html:
An ancient highway of the Achaemenid Persian Empire that ran about 2,700 kilometres from Susa in western Iran to Sardis near the Aegean coast of Anatolia. Darius the Great rebuilt and organised it around 500 BCE, joining older roads used by the Assyrians.

Along the way stood more than a hundred stations with inns, guards and fresh horses. Royal messengers rode in relays, each handing on to the next, so a message could cover the whole road in about a week instead of three months on foot. Herodotus admired them: nothing stopped them, he wrote, not snow, rain, heat or night. A version of his line is now the unofficial motto of the United States Postal Service.

The road held the huge empire together, moving orders, tax and troops. Alexander the Great marched along parts of it when he conquered Persia, and later routes such as the Silk Road reused sections of it.
